analysis.one_liner: Bans pricing algorithms trained on rivals' secret data to fix prices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote after a Democratic senator introduced it in January 2024.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to use or sell a pricing algorithm trained with nonpublic competitor data — the kind of software that lets companies in the same market feed each other's secret pricing information into a computer and end up charging similar higher prices. It would give antitrust enforcers power to audit these algorithms, create a legal presumption that selling one algorithm to multiple competitors is price fixing, require large companies to tell customers and workers when an algorithm sets their price or pay, and order a federal study of the practice.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who could pay lower prices if algorithms that pool competitors' private data can no longer push prices up together. Workers also get a small protection: the bill treats pay as a 'price,' so algorithms that coordinate pay across employers or discriminate between similar workers would be covered, and workers would be told when an algorithm sets their pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and workers facing algorithm-driven prices

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to use or distribute any pricing algorithm that uses, incorporates, or was trained with nonpublic competitor data, enforceable with civil penalties of at least $10,000 per day or the total sales price of everything sold with the algorithm [S2].

Creates a presumption under the Sherman Act that a defendant agreed to restrain trade if it distributed one pricing algorithm to two or more competitors in the same market, making algorithmic price fixing easier to prove in court [S2].

Lets the Justice Department and FTC demand, on 30 days' notice, a detailed report on any pricing algorithm — who built it, what data it uses, whether a human reviews its decisions, and whether it charges different customers different prices — certified by a corporate officer under penalty of perjury [S2].

Requires any company with $5 million or more in annual revenue to tell customers before purchase, and tell employees and contractors, when an algorithm sets or recommends their price or pay, with penalties of at least $5,000 per day for failures to disclose [S2].
Orders the FTC to study within two years how widely pricing algorithms are used, how often they produce price or wage discrimination, and where more oversight is needed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that use or sell pricing software, especially third-party providers whose products serve many competitors in the same market, and companies with $5 million or more in revenue that would face disclosure duties. The penalty structure is steep: a company could owe the full sales price of every product sold through a violating algorithm.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pricing software vendors and large algorithm users

drawbacks.text: The ban is written broadly: it covers any algorithm 'trained with' nonpublic competitor data, and the bill does not require proof that the algorithm actually raised prices — critics of similar proposals argue this could sweep in ordinary market-research data and legitimate dynamic pricing that matches supply and demand [S2].

Penalties are potentially out of proportion: a violator can owe not just a per-day fine but the sum of the price of every product or service sold using the algorithm, an amount that could exceed any actual overcharge to consumers [S2].

Compliance would be a real cost: companies above $5 million in revenue must make disclosures before every covered sale and be ready to produce detailed algorithm reports within 30 days, and executives must personally certify them under penalty of perjury [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If algorithmic collusion is as widespread as its sponsors contend, the consumer savings from breaking it up would likely outweigh the compliance costs, which fall mainly on the firms doing the pricing. The strongest honest objection is design, not purpose: the ban triggers on the data an algorithm was trained with rather than on proof of higher prices, and the all-sales penalty could punish far beyond demonstrated harm. A narrower version could capture the same misconduct with less collateral damage; this version never got far enough for the Senate to weigh that tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in January 2024, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 30, 2024, joined by Democratic Senators Wyden, Durbin, Blumenthal, Hirono, and Welch, for a total of six Democratic cosponsors [S2][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action of any kind recorded [S1][S4].
The Judiciary Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, the full Senate never debated or voted on it, and the bill expired at the end of the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pricing software vendors and the companies that use their tools are better off, because the rules that would have constrained their algorithms never took effect. Consumers are no worse off than before, but got none of the promised price relief either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pricing software vendors and their business customers

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Preventing Algorithmic Collusion Act and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Wyden, Durbin, Blumenthal, Hirono, and Welch
for.role: Cosponsors (with a sixth, bringing the total to 6 Democratic cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none of them moved it past committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.role: Chair, Senate Judiciary Committee; also a cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill but, as committee chair, never brought it up for consideration in the panel he led.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill never had the bipartisan backing that typically moves a bill out of committee.

industries.industry: Pricing algorithm and revenue-management software vendors
industries.note: These firms sell one pricing tool to many competitors in the same market — the core practice the bill outlaws when the tool is trained on nonpublic competitor data. Their business model depends on keeping that channel open, which is exactly what pushes prices up for customers.

industries.industry: Hotels, airlines, and rental housing operators using dynamic pricing
industries.note: Heavy users of shared pricing software would face liability and the new audit regime, and consumers renting rooms or apartments would be the direct beneficiaries if coordinated pricing stops.

Any firm over $5 million in revenue would owe pre-sale disclosures and algorithm reports, a real compliance cost, but firms using purely internal pricing data would remain free to keep algorithmic pricing.
